slides.title: Obligations and contracts: where real contracts fit
slides.text:
Lesson for the class of 18 November 2026 (Obligations; real contracts). Page references: "Oblig." = Benke/Meissel, Roman Law of Obligations; "Property" = Benke/Meissel, Roman Law of Property (2nd ed. transcript).

### Four ways to contract (Gai Inst 3.89)
Gaius says an obligation is contracted RE (by delivery of a thing), VERBIS (by words), LITTERIS (by an entry in a ledger) or CONSENSU (by consent). Whatever the mode, every contract rests on the parties' agreement (Oblig. p. 14).

| Group | How it arises | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Consensual | bare agreement (CONSENSUS) | sale, lease/work, mandate, partnership |
| Real | agreement + delivery of a thing | MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM, PIGNUS |
| Verbal | set question and answer | STIPULATIO ("SPONDESNE?" – "SPONDEO.") |
| Literal | ledger entry | CODEX ACCEPTI ET EXPENSI |

### What makes a contract "real"
A real contract needs CONVENTIO + DATIO (Oblig. p. 37). The CONVENTIO fixes the purpose of the transfer and so decides WHICH real contract it is. But the agreement alone is not enough: the obligation arises only when the thing is actually handed over (DATIO). Until then, there is no contract at all.

In principle all real contracts are GRATUITOUS. The one exception is the DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, where the recipient may use money and pays interest (Oblig. p. 37).

### Two kinds of action (Oblig. pp. 17–18)
- IUDICIA STRICTI IURIS: the formula gives the judge a narrow programme. Example: the lender's CONDICTIO from a MUTUUM. The judge only checks whether the sum was received as a loan; a defence such as an informal waiver needs an EXCEPTIO (e.g. EXCEPTIO PACTI, EXCEPTIO DOLI) in the formula.
- BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA: the judge assesses everything EX BONA FIDE and considers fraud, set-off or side agreements on his own motion. DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM and the contract of PIGNUS are judged this way.

### Who is bound (Oblig. p. 19)
MUTUUM is UNILATERALLY obliging: only the borrower owes something. DEPOSITUM and COMMODATUM are IMPERFECTLY BILATERAL: the recipient must always return the thing (ACTIO … DIRECTA), the giver owes something only if expenses or losses arise (ACTIO … CONTRARIA).

terms.def: The agreement at the core of every real contract; it fixes the purpose of the transfer and so the type of real contract (Oblig. p. 37).
The actual handing over of the thing; without it a real contract does not arise (Oblig. p. 37).
Action with a narrow formula, e.g. the CONDICTIO; defences must be pleaded as an EXCEPTIO (Oblig. pp. 17–18).
Action whose formula tells the judge to decide EX BONA FIDE, taking all circumstances into account without an EXCEPTIO (Oblig. pp. 17–18).

cards.q: What are the four ways of contracting according to Gai Inst 3.89?
cards.a:
RE (delivery of a thing), VERBIS (words), LITTERIS (ledger entry), CONSENSU (consent).
• Real contracts: MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM, PIGNUS
• Consensual: sale, LOCATIO CONDUCTIO, mandate, partnership (Oblig. pp. 14–15)

cards.q: What two elements create a real contract?
cards.a:
CONVENTIO (agreement on the purpose of the transfer) + DATIO (actual delivery of the thing).
• The CONVENTIO decides which real contract it is
• Without the DATIO there is no obligation, however clear the agreement (Oblig. p. 37)

cards.q: How does a real contract differ from a consensual contract?
cards.a:
A consensual contract arises from bare agreement (CONSENSUS); a real contract needs agreement PLUS delivery of the thing (DATIO).
• Sale = consensual; loan for consumption = real (Oblig. pp. 14–15, 37)

cards.q: BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA vs IUDICIA STRICTI IURIS: what is the practical difference?
cards.a:
In a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM the judge considers all circumstances (fraud, set-off, side agreements) on his own motion; in a IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS such defences need an EXCEPTIO in the formula.
• Stricti iuris: CONDICTIO from MUTUUM
• Bonae fidei: ACTIO DEPOSITI, COMMODATI, PIGNERATICIA (Oblig. pp. 17–18, 51, 60, 67)

cards.q: Which real contract is unilaterally obliging, and which are imperfectly bilateral?
cards.a:
MUTUUM is unilaterally obliging (only the borrower owes); DEPOSITUM and COMMODATUM are imperfectly bilateral.
• Return claim always arises (ACTIO DIRECTA)
• The giver owes only if expenses or losses occur (ACTIO CONTRARIA) (Oblig. pp. 19, 51, 60)

slides.title: Liability and risk: DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA, CASUS
slides.text:
In almost every fragment on a real contract the real question is: WHO BEARS THE LOSS when the thing is damaged, stolen or destroyed? You answer it with two tools: the standard of liability and the rules on risk.

### Degrees of fault (Oblig. p. 26)
- DOLUS: a breach committed knowing it harms the creditor (DOLUS MALUS = intent to harm). Liability for DOLUS can never be excluded by agreement.
- CULPA: falling short of the care the contract requires, without intent. CULPA LATA = gross negligence; CULPA LEVIS = slight negligence.
- DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS: the care one gives to one's own things. It is a subjective standard; breaching it is CULPA IN CONCRETO, breaching an objective standard is CULPA IN ABSTRACTO (Oblig. p. 53).

### Accident (Oblig. pp. 26–27)
- CASUS = loss nobody is at fault for. Default rule: CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS, the owner bears accidental loss.
- VIS MAIOR = what no one can foresee or control: earthquakes, robbers, pirates, the natural death of a slave. The debtor is generally not liable for it.
- CASUS MINOR = loss that special precautions (guarding) could have prevented, above all simple theft.

### CUSTODIA
If a contract imposes CUSTODIA, the debtor answers for typical guard-preventable loss, especially theft, without the creditor having to prove a breach of care. In effect this is strict liability; later jurists (Gaius and others) reinterpret it as liability for breaching a duty to guard (Oblig. p. 27).

### The utility principle (Oblig. p. 52)
Liability follows the interests: the party with the greater economic interest in the contract bears more risk. It works on two levels: (a) each contract type has a typical distribution of interests; (b) if the interests in the concrete case differ from the type, the risk is allocated differently.

| Contract | Whose interest? | Recipient liable for |
|---|---|---|
| DEPOSITUM | depositor | DOLUS, CULPA LATA, DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS |
| COMMODATUM | borrower | DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA |
| PIGNUS | pledgee | DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA |
| MUTUUM | borrower is owner | everything: repays regardless of fault |

Whoever uses a thing without permission is liable even for accidents that result from the use (CASUS MIXTUS; Oblig. pp. 54, 61–62).

terms.def: Intentional breach, knowing it harms the creditor; liability for it cannot be excluded (Oblig. p. 26).
Gross / slight negligence: falling short of the required care without intent (Oblig. p. 26).
The care a person gives to his own things; a subjective standard (CULPA IN CONCRETO), applied to the depositary (Oblig. p. 53).
Liability for typical guard-preventable loss, especially theft, without proof of fault; in effect strict liability (Oblig. p. 27).
Superior force that no one can foresee or control (earthquake, robbers, pirates); generally not the debtor's risk (Oblig. pp. 26–27).
The owner bears accidental loss of his thing (Oblig. p. 26).

cards.q: What is the difference between DOLUS and CULPA in contractual liability?
cards.a:
DOLUS = breach committed knowing it harms the creditor; CULPA = falling short of the required care without intent.
• CULPA LATA (gross) vs CULPA LEVIS (slight)
• Liability for DOLUS cannot be excluded (Oblig. p. 26)

cards.q: What does DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS mean, and for whom does it matter?
cards.a:
The care a person gives to his own things: a subjective standard; breaching it = CULPA IN CONCRETO.
• The depositary is liable if he treats the deposit worse than his own property (Celsus D 16.3.32, Case 12; Oblig. p. 53)

cards.q: What is CUSTODIA liability?
cards.a:
Liability for typical loss that guarding would prevent, especially theft, without the creditor proving a breach of care: in effect strict liability.
• Later reinterpreted as liability for breaching a duty to guard
• Borne by the commodatary and the pledgee (Oblig. pp. 27, 61, 67)

cards.q: VIS MAIOR vs CASUS MINOR: what is the difference?
cards.a:
VIS MAIOR = events no one can foresee or control (earthquake, robbers, pirates); CASUS MINOR = loss that special precautions could prevent, mainly theft (= the CUSTODIA area).
• The debtor is generally not liable for VIS MAIOR (Oblig. pp. 26–27)

cards.q: What is the utility principle?
cards.a:
Contractual liability follows the interests: the party with the greater economic interest bears more of the risk.
• Level 1: typical distribution of interests of the contract type
• Level 2: deviating interests in the concrete case shift the risk (Oblig. p. 52)

cards.q: What does CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS mean for real contracts?
cards.a:
The owner bears accidental loss.
• MUTUUM: the borrower becomes owner, so he bears the risk from delivery
• DEPOSITUM/COMMODATUM: the giver normally stays owner and bears accidental loss (Oblig. pp. 26, 40, 54, 61)

slides.title: Property law you need for real contracts
slides.text:
Real contracts sit on the border between obligations and property. A fragment on a loan or deposit almost always asks first: WHO OWNS and WHO POSSESSES the thing after the DATIO?

### Ownership, possession, detention
- OWNERSHIP (DOMINIUM) is the full right to a thing, protected by the REI VINDICATIO (Property pp. 68, 156).
- POSSESSION is a fact: control (CORPUS) plus the intent to hold the thing for oneself (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI) (Property pp. 12–14).
- DETENTION (NATURALIS POSSESSIO): holding a thing FOR ANOTHER. Typical detentors are tenants, depositaries and precarists (Property p. 15). The depositor keeps proprietary possession mediately, through the depositary (Property p. 16).

### What each real contract does in property law (Oblig. p. 37)
| Contract | Recipient becomes | Giver keeps |
|---|---|---|
| MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE | OWNER and possessor | only a claim (CONDICTIO / ACTIO DEPOSITI) |
| DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM, PIGNUS, PRECARIUM | DETENTOR (natural possessor) | ownership and possession |

MUTUUM passes ownership by TRADITIO, with the loan as IUSTA CAUSA (Oblig. p. 39; Property p. 85). So the lender must be owner or authorised: NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET (Oblig. p. 46). Among natural possessors, only emphyteutic lessees, precarists, pledgees and sequesters are listed as protected by possessory interdicts (Property p. 17).

### Changing the role without handing over
TRADITIO BREVI MANU: a detentor becomes possessor and owner by mere agreement, because he already holds the thing. A depositary allowed to use deposited coins as a loan thus becomes owner and borrower (Property p. 42; Oblig. pp. 44, 55).

### NUMMOS CONSUMERE
Whoever mixes another's coins indistinguishably with his own, or spends them in good faith, acquires ORIGINAL ownership, even a thief (Property p. 142). The former owner loses ownership.

### REI VINDICATIO vs CONDICTIO
- REI VINDICATIO: the owner's action IN REM against any possessor, only while the thing exists and he is still owner (Property p. 160).
- CONDICTIO: action IN PERSONAM for a certain sum or thing: the lender's action from MUTUUM, and the action for unjust enrichment (Oblig. pp. 33, 39). Against a thief: CONDICTIO FURTIVA (Property p. 22).

### PIGNUS: right in rem vs contract
The RIGHT of pledge arises from the CONVENTIO PIGNORIS without delivery (secured debt + pledger's power of disposal + agreement). The CONTRACT of pledge needs a DATIO and is valid even without power of disposal; the pledgee then has only contractual claims (Oblig. p. 66; Property p. 192).

terms.def: Holding a thing for another (ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI); the position of depositary, borrower for use, pledgee and precarist (Property p. 15; Oblig. p. 37).
Transfer of possession by agreement to a person who already holds the thing as detentor (Property p. 42).

terms.term: NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET
terms.def: No one can transfer more rights than he has (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr; Property p. 77).
Mixing another's coins indistinguishably with one's own or spending them in good faith; it gives original ownership (Property p. 142).
The owner's action in rem against any possessor of his thing: UBI REM MEAM INVENIO, IBI VINDICO (Property p. 160).
Action in personam for a certain sum or thing; the lender's action and the claim for unjust enrichment (Oblig. pp. 33, 39).

cards.q: After the DATIO, who owns and who possesses in a MUTUUM compared with a DEPOSITUM?
cards.a:
MUTUUM: the borrower becomes OWNER and possessor; DEPOSITUM: the depositary is only a DETENTOR (natural possessor), the depositor keeps ownership and (mediate) possession.
• Same for COMMODATUM, PIGNUS: recipient = detentor
• DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE: recipient becomes owner (Oblig. p. 37; Property pp. 15–16)

cards.q: By which act and on which IUSTA CAUSA does ownership pass in a MUTUUM?
cards.a:
By TRADITIO, with the loan (MUTUUM) as IUSTA CAUSA.
• The lender must be owner or authorised (NEMO PLUS IURIS)
• Repayment again transfers ownership back to the lender (Oblig. p. 39; Property p. 85)

cards.q: What is TRADITIO BREVI MANU, and how does it turn a deposit into a loan?
cards.a:
A detentor becomes possessor (and owner) by agreement alone, since he already holds the thing.
• Depositor allows the depositary to use deposited coins as a loan: the depositary moves from detention to proprietary possession and acquires ownership with the loan as causa → MUTUUM (Property p. 42; Oblig. pp. 44, 55)

cards.q: What is NUMMOS CONSUMERE, and what does it do to the former owner's remedies?
cards.a:
Mixing another's coins indistinguishably with one's own or spending them in good faith: the user acquires ORIGINAL ownership (even a thief).
• The former owner loses the REI VINDICATIO
• He keeps only personal claims: CONDICTIO, or CONDICTIO FURTIVA against a thief (Property p. 142)

cards.q: REI VINDICATIO vs CONDICTIO: when does the giver of a thing use which?
cards.a:
REI VINDICATIO (in rem) while he is still owner and the thing exists; CONDICTIO (in personam) when ownership has passed or been lost, e.g. after a MUTUUM or after the coins were consumed.
• REI VINDICATIO lies against any possessor (Property p. 160)

cards.q: What is the difference between the right of pledge and the real contract of pledge (PIGNUS)?
cards.a:
The right of pledge (in rem) arises from the CONVENTIO PIGNORIS without delivery; the real contract needs a DATIO.
• Right in rem requires: secured debt, pledger's power of disposal, CONVENTIO PIGNORIS
• The contract is valid even without power of disposal; the pledgee then has only contractual claims (Oblig. p. 66; Property p. 192)

slides.title: MUTUUM — the loan for consumption
slides.text:
### Definition (Oblig. pp. 37–38)
MUTUUM arises when the lender transfers OWNERSHIP of money or other fungibles (things dealt in by number, weight or measure: coins, grain, olives) to the borrower, who must return not the same pieces but TANTUNDEM EIUSDEM GENERIS, the same quantity of the same kind. It is interest-free and unilaterally obliging.

### Five requirements (Oblig. p. 38)
1. a CONVENTIO of loan;
2. actual delivery (DATIO);
3. fungible things;
4. the lender is owner or entitled to dispose;
5. the borrower acquires ownership.

Requirements 4 and 5 are the property-law test: if the lender is not owner, the borrower cannot become owner, and no MUTUUM arises (see mini exegesis 1).

### Risk
The borrower is owner, so from delivery he alone bears the risk: he must repay regardless of fault (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS; Oblig. pp. 38, 40). Contrast the maritime loan (FENUS NAUTICUM): if the ship is lost, the borrower need not repay.

### Action (Oblig. pp. 39–40)
The lender sues with the CONDICTIO, a IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS: for money also called ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE, for produce CONDICTIO TRITICARIA. He needs to prove only the delivery, which makes it a very efficient remedy. The condictio covers only TANTUNDEM, never interest; interest needed a STIPULATIO. Against a lender in blatant bad faith the borrower needs an EXCEPTIO DOLI.

### CONVENTIO and DATIO together: Ulpian (Proculus) D 12.1.11.1 (Case 1)
A hands B 10 coins, agreed debt 9: loan of 9. Agreed debt 11: loan of 10 only, because the DATIO covers only 10; the 11th coin needs a STIPULATIO (Oblig. pp. 40–41).

### Special forms (Oblig. pp. 41–45)
- Loan by assignment: the lender has a third party pay the borrower (classical, accepted).
- Loan by agreement: a debtor may keep owed money as a loan; Ulpian (D 12.1.15) yes, Julian (D 17.1.34 pr) no.
- CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE: the lender gives goods to sell, the proceeds to be kept as a loan; Ulpian sees a MUTUUM once sold, Julian denies it.

### SC MACEDONIANUM (Oblig. pp. 47–49)
Loans to sons and daughters in PATRIA POTESTAS: the lender's CONDICTIO is refused or defeated by the EXCEPTIO SC MACEDONIANI; a natural obligation remains, so payment made cannot be reclaimed.

terms.def: Interest-free loan for consumption: ownership of fungibles passes to the borrower, who returns the same quantity of the same kind (Oblig. pp. 37–38).
'As much of the same kind': the borrower's duty of return in a MUTUUM (Oblig. p. 38).
The CONDICTIO for a specific lent sum of money (Oblig. p. 39).
Goods handed over to be sold, the proceeds to be kept as a loan (Oblig. pp. 41, 43).
Senate decree (69–79 AD) blocking the lender's CONDICTIO for loans to children in PATRIA POTESTAS (Oblig. p. 47).

cards.q: What is MUTUUM?
cards.a:
An interest-free loan for consumption: the lender transfers OWNERSHIP of fungibles (money, grain) and the borrower returns TANTUNDEM EIUSDEM GENERIS, not the same pieces.
• Real contract, unilaterally obliging, gratuitous (Oblig. pp. 37–38)

cards.q: What are the five requirements of a MUTUUM?
cards.a:
1. CONVENTIO of loan
• 2. DATIO; 3. fungible things
• 4. lender is owner or entitled to dispose; 5. borrower acquires ownership (Oblig. p. 38)

cards.q: Which action does the lender in a MUTUUM have, and what are its features?
cards.a:
The CONDICTIO (for money: ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE), a IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS.
• Only delivery must be proved: a fast, efficient remedy
• Covers only TANTUNDEM, no interest; interest needs a STIPULATIO (Oblig. pp. 39–40)

cards.q: Who bears the risk of accidental loss in a MUTUUM, and why?
cards.a:
The borrower, from delivery: he is owner, so he must repay regardless of fault (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS).
• Before the DATIO the lender bears it
• Contrast FENUS NAUTICUM: no repayment if the ship is lost (Oblig. pp. 38, 40)

cards.q: Ulpian (Proculus) D 12.1.11.1 (Case 1): A hands B 10 coins; the agreed debt is 9, or 11. How much is owed as a loan?
cards.a:
9 in the first case (the CONVENTIO limits it); 10 in the second (the DATIO limits it).
• A loan never exceeds what was delivered; for the 11th coin a STIPULATIO is needed
• A 10th coin repaid by mistake can be reclaimed by CONDICTIO INDEBITI (Oblig. pp. 40–41)

cards.q: What is the effect of the SC MACEDONIANUM on a loan to a son in power?
cards.a:
The lender's CONDICTIO is refused or defeated by the EXCEPTIO SC MACEDONIANI; only a natural obligation remains.
• Repayment made cannot be reclaimed
• No protection if the PATER FAMILIAS approved, or if the son posed as SUI IURIS (Oblig. pp. 47–48)

slides.title: DEPOSITUM — safekeeping
slides.text:
### Definition (Oblig. p. 51)
DEPOSITUM arises when a thing is handed over to someone who agrees to keep it GRATUITOUSLY. The very same thing must be returned; fungibles can be deposited too. Unlike MUTUUM, it does not matter whether the depositor owns the thing.
- The depositary may NOT use the thing; unauthorised use is FURTUM (Gai Inst 3.196).
- Paid safekeeping is LOCATIO CONDUCTIO, not DEPOSITUM.

### Actions (Oblig. pp. 51–52)
BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM, imperfectly bilateral:
- depositor: ACTIO DEPOSITI DIRECTA, above all for return;
- depositary: ACTIO DEPOSITI CONTRARIA for expenses and losses caused by the deposit (e.g. feed, or a contagious disease infecting his own animals). He may keep the thing until paid, without an EXCEPTIO DOLI. He can even claim upkeep costs within the depositor's action (Modestinus Coll 10.2.5, Case 31; Oblig. p. 65).

### Liability (Oblig. pp. 53–54)
Safekeeping is a favour, so the depositary is liable only for DOLUS, extended by classical jurists to CULPA LATA and to DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS (Nerva and Celsus D 16.3.32, Case 12). The depositor bears CULPA LEVIS and CASUS (as owner). Heightened liability:
- if the depositary pressed his services on the depositor, he answers for DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA (Ulpian D 16.3.1.35, Case 14);
- if he dolosely uses the deposit, he bears accidents resulting from the use (CASUS MIXTUS; Ulpian D 16.3.1.25, Case 15).

### Deposits of money (Oblig. pp. 54–59)
- A sealed bag of coins is an ordinary deposit: the same bag goes back.
- DEPOSIT → LOAN: if the depositor later permits use, the new CONVENTIO plus TRADITIO BREVI MANU at once creates a MUTUUM (Ulpian D 12.1.9.9, Case 16). But if permission is given at the time of depositing, the loan arises only when the money is actually taken out (Ulpian D 12.1.10, Case 17).
- DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE: money deposited with permission to use it, often open (not sealed). Ownership passes, the recipient repays regardless of fault and may owe interest, depending on the terms; the giver sues with the ACTIO DEPOSITI (bonae fidei), which can take in interest (Paulus D 16.3.29.1, Case 18; Scaevola D 16.3.28, Case 20b).

### DEPOSITUM SEQUESTRE (Oblig. p. 59)
Litigants deposit the disputed thing with a SEQUESTER, who hands it to the winner. He is protected by interdicts; the winner sues with the ACTIO DEPOSITI SEQUESTRARIA.

terms.def: Gratuitous safekeeping of a thing handed over; the same thing must be returned (Oblig. p. 51).
Depositor's action for return / depositary's action for expenses and losses; both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA (Oblig. pp. 51–52).
Money deposited with permission to use it: ownership passes, interest is owed, ACTIO DEPOSITI (Oblig. pp. 56–57).
Accidental loss that follows an unauthorised use; the user is liable for it (Oblig. p. 54).
Third person with whom litigants deposit the disputed thing until judgment (Oblig. p. 59).

cards.q: What is DEPOSITUM?
cards.a:
A real contract by which a thing is handed over to be kept GRATUITOUSLY and returned as the very same thing.
• The depositary may not use it (use = FURTUM)
• Ownership of the depositor irrelevant; paid safekeeping = LOCATIO CONDUCTIO (Oblig. p. 51)

cards.q: What are the depositary's standards of liability?
cards.a:
DOLUS, extended to CULPA LATA and to DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS; the depositor bears CULPA LEVIS and CASUS.
• If the depositary pressed his services: DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA
• Dolose use: CASUS MIXTUS (Oblig. pp. 53–54)

cards.q: Which actions arise from DEPOSITUM, and of what type are they?
cards.a:
ACTIO DEPOSITI DIRECTA (depositor: return) and ACTIO DEPOSITI CONTRARIA (depositary: expenses, losses); both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.
• Depositary may retain the thing until paid without an EXCEPTIO DOLI (Oblig. pp. 51–52)

cards.q: DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE vs MUTUUM: what do they share and how do they differ?
cards.a:
Both pass ownership of money and the recipient must repay regardless of fault; but DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE serves the giver's interest in safety, is sued with the ACTIO DEPOSITI (bonae fidei), which can include interest.
• MUTUUM: CONDICTIO (stricti iuris), no interest (Oblig. pp. 37, 56–57)

cards.q: Ulpian D 12.1.9.9 (Case 16) vs Ulpian D 12.1.10 (Case 17): when does a deposit of money become a loan?
cards.a:
D 12.1.9.9: permission to use given LATER → the loan arises at once with the changed CONVENTIO and TRADITIO BREVI MANU.
• D 12.1.10: permission given AT the deposit → the loan arises only when the money is actually taken out (Oblig. pp. 55–59)

slides.title: COMMODATUM, PRECARIUM and the contract of PIGNUS
slides.text:
### COMMODATUM — loan for use (Oblig. pp. 60–61)
The lender (commodator) hands over a thing so that the borrower (commodatary) may USE it free of charge and return the very same thing. Only non-consumables can be lent; the lender need not be owner. A paid loan for use is a lease (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI). Use beyond what was agreed (or what BONA FIDES allows) is FURTUM.

Actions (BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA): ACTIO COMMODATI DIRECTA for return; ACTIO COMMODATI CONTRARIA for the borrower's extraordinary expenses and losses. The borrower carries ordinary running costs, e.g. fodder; necessary vet costs for an illness unrelated to the use are reimbursed (Modestinus Coll 10.2.5, Case 31).

Liability: the loan benefits only the borrower, so he is liable for DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA; the lender, as owner, bears VIS MAIOR (Oblig. p. 61). Gaius D 13.6.18 pr (Case 23):
1. liable for fault, not for VIS MAIOR;
2. but liable even for VIS MAIOR if he used the thing beyond the permission (silver taken on a journey and lost to pirates);
3. where the lender also has an interest, liability is lower: CULPA (Gaius); only DOLUS where the loan served solely the lender (Ulpian D 13.6.5.10, Case 25).

Because he bears CUSTODIA, the borrower (not the owner) has the ACTIO FURTI against a thief, unless he is insolvent (Modestinus Coll 10.2.6, Case 28). He is generally not liable for damage done by a third party (Julian D 13.6.19, Case 27; Marcellus dissenting).

### PRECARIUM (Oblig. pp. 65–66)
A factual grant of use, revocable by the grantor at any time, usually at the recipient's request. The jurists saw the parallels to COMMODATUM but treated it as a factual arrangement, NOT a contract. The precarist is protected by possessory interdicts, but not against the grantor (EXCEPTIO VITIOSAE POSSESSIONIS); the grantor recovers by the INTERDICTUM DE PRECARIO.

### PIGNUS as a real contract (Oblig. pp. 66–67)
A thing is given as security for a debt. The pledgee may not use it (FURTUM), except in antichresis. Actions (bonae fidei):
- pledger: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM DIRECTA for return after the debt ends, or for the surplus of the sale proceeds (SUPERFLUUM, HYPEROCHA);
- pledgee: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM CONTRARIA for expenses and damage, and for a substitute pledge if no right in rem arose.
The pledge serves only the pledgee, so he is liable for DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA.

terms.def: Gratuitous loan for use of a non-consumable thing; the same thing is returned (Oblig. p. 60).
Lender's action for return / borrower's action for extraordinary expenses and losses; BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA (Oblig. p. 60).
Factual grant of use revocable at any time; not a contract; grantor's remedy INTERDICTUM DE PRECARIO (Oblig. pp. 65–66).

terms.term: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM DIRECTA / CONTRARIA
terms.def: Pledger's action for return or surplus / pledgee's action for expenses, damage or a substitute pledge (Oblig. p. 67).
Surplus of the sale proceeds over the secured debt, owed to the pledger (Oblig. p. 67).

cards.q: What is COMMODATUM?
cards.a:
A real contract: a non-consumable thing is handed over for gratuitous USE and the very same thing must be returned.
• Lender need not be owner
• Paid = LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI; use beyond the agreement = FURTUM (Oblig. p. 60)

cards.q: What is the commodatary liable for, and what does the lender bear?
cards.a:
The borrower: DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA, because the loan benefits only him; the lender bears VIS MAIOR as owner.
• Excess use: borrower liable even for VIS MAIOR
• Lender also interested: lower liability (Oblig. pp. 61–62)

cards.q: COMMODATUM vs DEPOSITUM: how do they differ in use, liability and costs?
cards.a:
COMMODATUM: recipient may use; liable for DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA; bears ordinary upkeep. DEPOSITUM: no use; liable only for DOLUS (+ CULPA LATA, DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS); upkeep reimbursed.
• Both: same thing returned, gratuitous, bonae fidei, recipient = detentor (Oblig. pp. 51–53, 60–61, 65)

cards.q: Gaius D 13.6.18 pr (Case 23): what three rules does Gaius state on the commodatary's liability?
cards.a:
1. Liable for fault, not for VIS MAIOR.
• 2. Liable even for VIS MAIOR if he used the thing beyond the permission (silver taken on a journey, lost to pirates)
• 3. If both parties have an interest: liable only for CULPA (Oblig. pp. 61–62)

cards.q: What is PRECARIUM, and how does the grantor get the thing back?
cards.a:
A factual grant of use revocable at any time, usually at the recipient's request; not a contract.
• Precarist protected by interdicts, but not against the grantor (EXCEPTIO VITIOSAE POSSESSIONIS)
• Grantor: INTERDICTUM DE PRECARIO; unlike COMMODATUM, no actions in personam (Oblig. pp. 65–66; Property p. 17)

cards.q: Which actions arise from the real contract of pledge, and what is the pledgee liable for?
cards.a:
Pledger: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM DIRECTA (return, or SUPERFLUUM); pledgee: CONTRARIA (expenses, damage, substitute pledge).
• Both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA
• Pledgee liable for DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA (utility principle) (Oblig. p. 67)

slides.title: Mini exegesis 1: Ulpian D 12.1.13 pr (stolen money lent)
slides.text:
Benke/Meissel, Obligations Case 6 (pp. 46–47). The facts below follow the textbook's summary; read the full text in Watson's translation before class.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: G steals money from E. G lends this money to N, who takes it in good faith as a loan. N then spends the money.
2. Legal question: Can a loan for consumption arise between G and N, although G was not owner of the coins? Once N has spent the money, can repayment be claimed from him?
3. Decision: Author: ULPIAN. Once N has spent the money, a CONDICTIO lies against N. According to Benke/Meissel it presumably lies in G's hands (p. 46).

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: MUTUUM. CONVENTIO and DATIO are present, but requirements 4 and 5 fail: the thief is not owner, so N cannot become owner (NEMO PLUS IURIS). At first there is NO MUTUUM.
5. Claims and remedies, stage by stage:

| Stage | E (owner, victim) | G (thief, "lender") |
|---|---|---|
| Before N spends | still owner; N only possessor → REI VINDICATIO v N | no claim v N: no MUTUUM, and no enrichment CONDICTIO (his payment was neither mistaken nor on a defective causa) |
| After N spends | ownership lost; v G: ACTIO FURTI and CONDICTIO FURTIVA | CONDICTIO v N (Ulpian) |

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
6. Property law decides the case: by mixing the coins with his own or paying them on in good faith, N acquires ORIGINAL ownership (NUMMOS CONSUMERE; Property p. 142). E's REI VINDICATIO is gone, because he is no longer owner.
7. Why a CONDICTIO now? Consuming the coins gives N their economic value: practically the same position as if he had become owner by DATIO. Ulpian appears to let this cure the defective loan (convalescence) (p. 47).
8. Interests: the aim is probably to protect the victim E, not the thief or N. With a condiction against (presumably solvent) N, E can make the thief assign it to him; that is better than relying only on ACTIO FURTI and CONDICTIO FURTIVA against a possibly insolvent thief (p. 47).
9. Similar case: Ulpian D 12.1.18 pr (Model exegesis 2 in "How to write an exegesis"): coins received without a valid causa, ownership acquired only by consumption, then a CONDICTIO.

terms.def: Owner's reipersecutory action against the thief for the thing or its value, even if the thing has perished (Property p. 22).
Penal action for theft: twofold or fourfold value; may be cumulated with the CONDICTIO FURTIVA (Property p. 22).
A defective legal position is cured by a later event; here the consumption of the coins cures the defective loan (Oblig. p. 47).

cards.q: D 12.1.13 pr — What are the facts?
cards.a: Thief G lends money stolen from E to N, who takes it in good faith as a loan and then spends it (Case 6).

cards.q: D 12.1.13 pr — What is the legal question, and what does Ulpian decide?
cards.a:
Can a loan arise although the 'lender' was not owner, and can repayment be claimed after N has spent the money?
• Ulpian: once N has spent the money, a CONDICTIO lies against N
• Benke/Meissel: presumably held by G (Oblig. p. 46)

cards.q: D 12.1.13 pr — Why is there at first no MUTUUM between G and N?
cards.a:
The thief is not owner, so N cannot become owner (NEMO PLUS IURIS): requirements 4 and 5 of the MUTUUM fail.
• CONVENTIO and DATIO are present
• Before spending, E can vindicate the coins from N (Oblig. p. 46)

cards.q: D 12.1.13 pr — Why does Ulpian allow a CONDICTIO once N has spent the money?
cards.a:
Spending or mixing gives N original ownership (NUMMOS CONSUMERE) and the coins' economic value: practically as if he had acquired by DATIO, so the loan is cured (convalescence).
• E's REI VINDICATIO is gone; E keeps ACTIO FURTI and CONDICTIO FURTIVA v G (Oblig. pp. 46–47; Property p. 142)

slides.title: Mini exegesis 2: Africanus (Julian) D 17.1.34 pr (procurator keeps money as a loan)
slides.text:
Benke/Meissel, Obligations Case 4 (pp. 44–45). The facts below follow the textbook's summary; read the full text in Watson's translation before class.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: P manages L's affairs as his procurator and collects money from L's debtors. Wanting to use the money himself for a while, P writes to L proposing that L lend it to him at 6 % interest. L agrees.
2. Legal question: Has a loan for consumption arisen between L and P, so that L can sue with the CONDICTIO (ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE)? If not, how can L recover the money and the interest?
3. Decision: Author AFRICANUS, reporting JULIAN. No MUTUUM and no condictio. But L can sue P with the ACTIO MANDATI for the money and the interest. Julian adds that the CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE is likewise no MUTUUM. On risk, Julian (applying the utility principle, as Benke/Meissel explain) puts it on P: he must repay even if the money is lost by accident (p. 45).

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institutions: MUTUUM (real contract) and MANDATUM (consensual contract, BONAE FIDEI).
5. Why no MUTUUM: there is no DATIO, and mere agreement (NUDA PACTIONE) cannot create one. Nor can TRADITIO BREVI MANU: P already was proprietary possessor and owner of the collected money. Nor is it a loan by assignment: that needs a loan CONVENTIO BEFORE the third party pays (pp. 44–45).
6. Remedy: the deferred handover is a consensual change of the mandate, so the ACTIO MANDATI lies. As a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM it also covers the 6 % interest, which a condictio never could. The price: every circumstance that might weaken L's claim can be raised before the judge (p. 45).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Controversy: Ulpian D 12.1.15 (Case 2), on very similar facts, says it IS a MUTUUM and grants the condictio. An agreement between creditor and debtor suffices without a physical DATIO, by analogy with the loan by assignment. It is a shortcut: strictly, B would hand the money to A, who would hand it straight back (pp. 42–43).
8. Similar case: Ulpian D 12.1.9.9 (Case 16): a depositary is allowed to use deposited coins; here TRADITIO BREVI MANU works, because a depositary is only detentor (p. 55).
9. Interests: the loan serves only P, so P bears the risk (utility principle); Julian's route gives L the interest but costs him the fast condictio procedure.

terms.def: Agent who manages another's affairs; here he collected money for his principal (Oblig. p. 44).
Bare agreement; for Julian it cannot replace the DATIO of a MUTUUM (Oblig. p. 44).
Action from the consensual contract of mandate; a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM that can include agreed interest (Oblig. p. 45).

cards.q: D 17.1.34 pr — What are the facts?
cards.a: Procurator P has collected money from L's debtors; he proposes by letter that L lend it to him at 6 % interest, and L agrees (Case 4).

cards.q: D 17.1.34 pr — What does Julian decide?
cards.a:
No MUTUUM and no CONDICTIO, but L can sue P with the ACTIO MANDATI for the money and the interest.
• The CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE is likewise no MUTUUM
• P bears the risk of accidental loss (Oblig. pp. 44–45)

cards.q: D 17.1.34 pr — Why is there no MUTUUM, and why does TRADITIO BREVI MANU not help?
cards.a:
There is no DATIO; mere agreement (NUDA PACTIONE) cannot create one.
• P already was proprietary possessor and owner of the collected money, so no TRADITIO BREVI MANU between him and L was possible
• Not a loan by assignment: the CONVENTIO came only after payment (Oblig. pp. 44–45)

cards.q: D 17.1.34 pr — What does L gain and lose by suing with the ACTIO MANDATI instead of the CONDICTIO?
cards.a:
Gain: as a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM it covers the agreed 6 % interest, which the condictio cannot.
• Loss: every circumstance that might weaken the claim can be raised before the judge (Oblig. p. 45)

cards.q: D 17.1.34 pr vs D 12.1.15 — What is the controversy between Julian and Ulpian on the loan by agreement?
cards.a:
Julian: no MUTUUM without a physical DATIO → ACTIO MANDATI. Ulpian: agreement between creditor and debtor suffices → MUTUUM and CONDICTIO.
• Ulpian argues by analogy with the loan by assignment, a shortcut of two transfers (Oblig. pp. 42–45)

slides.title: Mini exegesis 3: Ulpian (Labeo) D 13.6.5.14 (silver left at the host's house)
slides.text:
Benke/Meissel, Obligations Case 24 (pp. 62–63). The facts below follow the textbook's summary; read the full text in Watson's translation before class.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: T asks E to lay a table for him and to lend him silverware for it; E does so. T asks for the same the next day. So as not to carry the silver home, E leaves it at T's house, where it is destroyed overnight.
2. Legal question: Who bears the loss of the silver: E, the lender, or T, in whose house it was kept?
3. Decision: Author ULPIAN, citing LABEO. Labeo: if E sent someone to guard the silver, E bears the loss; if E posted no guard, T is liable. Ulpian recommends the ACTIO COMMODATI: the borrower is in general liable for CUSTODIA (and so also DOLUS and CULPA); a different allocation must be expressly agreed.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institutions: MANDATUM (laying the table) and COMMODATUM (lending the silver). Overnight, T does not use the silver, so one might call it a DEPOSITUM; this changes nothing, because that deposit is then in the depositary's interest, and he is liable (p. 63).
5. Claims: E v T for the value of the silver; legal basis: T's contractual liability. T v E: E bears the loss, as owner (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS) or because he took over the guarding.
6. Remedy: ACTIO COMMODATI (DIRECTA), a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Liability standard: under the utility principle the commodatary bears DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA; the lender bears VIS MAIOR (p. 61). Labeo's guard test fits the idea that controlling the thing means taking over the risk: by posting his own guard, E assumed it (p. 62).
8. Problem of interpretation: Ulpian's reference to CUSTODIA suggests loss by theft or the borrower's negligence. Labeo speaks of PERICULUM and may mean VIS MAIOR; but then making the borrower liable when no guard was posted does not fit the general commodate rules on risk (p. 63). Say this openly in the exam.
9. Similar cases: Gaius D 13.6.18 pr (Case 23): no liability for VIS MAIOR, except after excess use; Ulpian D 13.6.12.1 (Case 29): the lender's slave fetches the item and runs off; whether the loan had ended decides the risk. Julian D 13.6.19 (Case 27): the borrower is generally not liable for damage done by a third party.

terms.def: Risk of accidental loss; who bears it is a matter of risk allocation, not of fault (Oblig. pp. 26, 63).
Consensual, gratuitous contract to carry out a task for another; here laying the table (Oblig. pp. 14, 62).

cards.q: D 13.6.5.14 — What are the facts?
cards.a: E lays T's table and lends him silver; T asks for the same the next day, so E leaves the silver at T's house, where it is destroyed overnight (Case 24).

cards.q: D 13.6.5.14 — What do Labeo and Ulpian decide?
cards.a:
Labeo: if E posted a guard, E bears the loss; if not, T is liable.
• Ulpian: ACTIO COMMODATI; the borrower is in general liable for CUSTODIA (and DOLUS, CULPA); any other allocation must be expressly agreed (Oblig. pp. 62–63)

cards.q: D 13.6.5.14 — Which contracts are involved, and does it matter that the silver was not used overnight?
cards.a:
Mandate (laying the table) and COMMODATUM (lending the silver).
• Overnight one might see a DEPOSITUM, but it changes nothing: that deposit is in the depositary's interest, so he is liable (Oblig. pp. 62–63)

cards.q: D 13.6.5.14 — Why do Labeo's and Ulpian's views fit together only partly?
cards.a:
Ulpian's CUSTODIA points to theft or negligence; Labeo speaks of PERICULUM and may mean VIS MAIOR, which under the general commodate rules is the lender's risk.
• Posting his own guard = E took over the risk (Oblig. pp. 62–63)

slides.title: Exegesis checklist: a fragment on a real contract
slides.text:
Use the four steps of "How to write an exegesis" (facts, legal question, decision, interpretation). For a real contract, the interpretation should answer these questions in this order.

### 1. Which contract? Read the CONVENTIO
| Question | Answer → contract |
|---|---|
| Same kind and quantity returned, ownership passes? | MUTUUM |
| Same thing kept for the giver, no use? | DEPOSITUM |
| Money given with permission to use, interest? | DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE |
| Same thing used free of charge? | COMMODATUM |
| Use revocable at any time, no contract? | PRECARIUM |
| Thing given as security? | PIGNUS |
| Any of these against payment? | LOCATIO CONDUCTIO, not a real contract |

### 2. Was there a DATIO, and when?
No DATIO, no real contract. Watch for substitutes: TRADITIO BREVI MANU, loan by assignment, loan by agreement (Julian v Ulpian), CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE (Oblig. pp. 41–45).

### 3. Property status after the DATIO
Who is owner, who is possessor, who is only detentor? Was the giver owner (NEMO PLUS IURIS)? Have coins been mixed or spent (NUMMOS CONSUMERE)? This decides REI VINDICATIO v CONDICTIO.

### 4. Claims and actions
State A v B AND B v A: CONDICTIO (stricti iuris) for MUTUUM; ACTIO DEPOSITI / COMMODATI / PIGNERATICIA DIRECTA and CONTRARIA (bonae fidei); ACTIO FURTI for unauthorised use or theft; interdicts for the precarist and the grantor. Is an EXCEPTIO needed (stricti iuris) or not (bonae fidei)?

### 5. Liability and risk
Standard by the utility principle: depositary DOLUS (+ CULPA LATA, DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS); commodatary and pledgee DOLUS, CULPA, CUSTODIA; borrower in MUTUUM everything. Then check deviations: interests of the concrete case, unauthorised use (CASUS MIXTUS), express agreement. Who bears VIS MAIOR (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS)?

### 6. Controversy, similar cases, interests
Name the jurists who disagree (Julian v Ulpian on loans by agreement; Labeo v Ulpian on the silver), cite one or two parallel fragments, and explain the decision by the interests of the parties: who gains from the contract, who could have prevented the loss.

terms.def: Consensual contract of lease, services or work; paid safekeeping or paid use falls under it, not under a real contract (Oblig. pp. 51, 60).

cards.q: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about a real contract — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.a:
Which contract (CONVENTIO), was there a DATIO, and who owns or possesses afterwards?
• Claims both ways + actions (CONDICTIO or DIRECTA/CONTRARIA; EXCEPTIO needed?)
• Liability standard by utility principle and its deviations; who bears VIS MAIOR?
• Controversy, similar cases, interests

cards.q: How do you tell MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM and PRECARIUM apart from the facts?
cards.a:
Same kind returned and ownership passes = MUTUUM; same thing kept without use = DEPOSITUM; same thing used free = COMMODATUM; use revocable at will, no contract = PRECARIUM.
• Against payment: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO
• Thing as security: PIGNUS (Oblig. pp. 37–38, 51, 60, 65–66)

cards.q: In an exegesis, why must you check the property position before choosing the action?
cards.a:
Because it decides whether the giver still has the REI VINDICATIO (still owner) or only a CONDICTIO / contractual action (ownership passed or lost).
• MUTUUM: ownership passes → CONDICTIO
• Consumed coins: original acquisition → no REI VINDICATIO (Oblig. pp. 37, 46; Property pp. 142, 160)
